passage: There was one bicycle, half an hour of light left, and two boys who had stopped speaking at lunch. Anirban sat on the step outside the ration shop, calmer after the long walk home. Jeevan leaned on the handlebars. "You cheat every time," Anirban had shouted earlier. Now he tried again, slower. "When you took the cycle first, I felt cheated. I'd been waiting since morning." Jeevan scuffed the dust. "I felt bad when you yelled. I didn't know you were waiting." They watched the sky go orange. "Two rounds to the temple each, then swap?" Jeevan said. "And whoever's second rings the bell." Anirban laughed. Both of them rode lighter that evening.

Last week Chetan and I had a big fight over the class computer. I said he cheats because he always gets more time.
After Sir made us sit apart and drink water, I didn't feel like shouting any more. So when Sir asked, I said, "I felt cheated because the timer wasn't on." I didn't say "he cheats" this time.
Chetan said, "I felt bad because nobody told me when to stop."
We made a rule: the kitchen timer on the desk, fifteen minutes each, and whoever finishes rings the bell for the other.
We tried it yesterday. It worked. I felt lighter walking home, like I'd put down a heavy bag. I'm Seema, and I think I'm better at this now.

Coach's note, under-11 football, Saturday

Last week Joseph and Keerthana argued in the huddle over who takes penalties, and I had them sit on opposite benches with their water bottles until they had cooled.
Today, before warm-up, they came to me together. Keerthana said, "I felt cheated when he took two in a row." Joseph said, "I felt like nobody trusted me to score."
They had worked out a rule on their own: they alternate, and whoever misses one passes the next to someone who hasn't had a go.
I wrote it on the whiteboard. Both of them stood straighter afterwards, and Keerthana high-fived Joseph after his goal in the second half.

qa.q: What did Keerthana and Joseph's new penalty rule say?
qa.a: They alternate, and whoever misses passes the next one to someone who hasn't had a go.

qa.q: What did Joseph say he felt about the penalties?
qa.a: He felt that nobody trusted him to score, which left him hurt and doubted.

qa.q: What was the turning point that allowed them to settle the argument?
qa.a: After cooling down they named their feelings, cheated and not trusted, instead of blaming, and chose a fair turn-taking rule themselves.

qa.q: What might Keerthana be experiencing when she high-fives Joseph?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and friendly again, since the rule made things fair and she no longer needs to fight for her turn.

grounding: A coach records two children naming their feelings after cooling down and agreeing a fair penalty rule, and both seem lighter.

Saturday

Me and Zubin had a fight about carrom again today. He kept taking two turns when he pocketed the queen, and I shouted "You cheat!" and he shouted back.

We both went home. After lunch I felt less angry. I went to Zubin's building and we sat on the steps. I didn't say "you cheat." I said, "I felt cheated when you took two turns. I didn't know that rule." He said his grandpa plays it that way.

So we made our own rule. You get one extra turn only if you cover the queen. We wrote it on a paper and stuck it under the board.

Then we played three games. I lost two. It was fine. I felt lighter, like after a big drink of water.

Vijay

qa.a: Saying "I felt cheated" instead of "You cheat" helped Zubin explain his grandpa's rule, so they could agree what was fair.

qa.a: Zubin was probably relieved and more willing to explain calmly, since Vijay spoke about feelings instead of blaming.
